questions.question: An object keeps doing what it is doing unless a _____ acts on it.
questions.explanation: This is the first law: without a (net) force, motion does not change.

questions.question: Is it true that a moving object needs a constant force to keep moving?
questions.explanation: With zero net force, a moving object keeps moving forever. Things on Earth slow down only because friction is a force acting against them.

questions.question: The tendency of an object to keep doing what it is already doing is called _____.
questions.explanation: Inertia is why passengers lurch forward when a bus brakes: their bodies keep moving.

questions.question: Force is measured in a unit called the _____.
questions.explanation: One newton (N) is the force that gives 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m/s².

questions.question: What is the net force on an object?
options: The biggest force acting on it
The total of all forces, with opposite directions subtracting
Only the force you push with
questions.explanation: The net force combines every force, taking direction into account. A is tempting, but smaller forces like friction also count.

questions.question: Is it true that an object can be moving even when the forces on it are balanced?
questions.explanation: Balanced forces mean no change in motion, so a moving object keeps moving at a steady speed in a straight line.

questions.question: If you double the net force on the same object, what happens to its acceleration?
questions.explanation: In a = F / m, acceleration grows in proportion to force. A is the mistake of mixing up force and mass.

questions.question: A net force of 10 N acts on a 2 kg object. What is its acceleration?
questions.explanation: a = F / m = 10 / 2 = 5 m/s². A is tempting, but it multiplies instead of dividing.

questions.question: Why does a heavy object speed up more slowly than a light one when pushed with the same force?
questions.answer: Because a = F / m: with the same force, a bigger mass gives a smaller acceleration.
questions.explanation: Because a = F / m: with the same force, a bigger mass gives a smaller acceleration. A full cart speeds up slower than an empty one.

questions.question: What does the third law say happens when you push on a wall?
questions.answer: The wall pushes back on you with a force of the same size in the opposite direction.
questions.explanation: The wall pushes back on you with a force of the same size in the opposite direction. That is why you feel the wall pressing on your hands.

questions.question: Is it true that the two forces of a third-law pair act on the same object?
questions.explanation: They act on two different objects: you push the cart, and the cart pushes you.

questions.question: Why don't the two forces of a third-law pair cancel each other out?
questions.answer: Because they act on two different objects, and forces only cancel when they act on the same object.
questions.explanation: Forces only cancel when they act on the same object. A third-law pair acts on two different objects, so each object feels its own force and can still move.
